title: The database decides when an index goes stale
subtitle: Index invalidation moved into SQL triggers and load-time checks, so a stale index cannot be served, and partial builds are failed before the daemon accepts its first connection
technologies: Idempotency, exactly-once effects and crash recovery

stats.label: triggers in the database that mark an index stale
load-time checks, in order, before a file is trusted

lede: An approximate index is a summary of the vectors it was built over. When those vectors change, the index is wrong, and a service that keeps serving it will return confident, stale neighbours with no error. The usual defence is a rule in the application: remember to rebuild. I put the rule in the database instead, where it cannot be forgotten, and backed it with checks at load time and at startup. Vectors live in append-only shards, each with a journal whose entry count advances on every append. A trigger on the catalog marks every active index that covers a shard as stale the moment that shard's journal count advances, with a reason attached.
quote: The write that changes the data is the write that invalidates the index.
evidence: Database-enforced invariants: index invalidation moved into PostgreSQL catalog triggers, so the write that changes vector data marks every covering index stale.
Fail-closed artifact loading: 3 ordered checks before an index file is trusted, kernel version, configuration hash and artifact hash, each mismatch a refusal with its reason.
Exactly-once delivery and crash recovery: partial index builds failed and their files removed before the daemon binds its listener, a sweep that is a no-op on a clean database.
Vector search and ANN indexes: search that loads only an active, checked index for a shard set and falls back to the general index, so a stale index is never a candidate.
author: Corey James
